papers.title_original: Neutralization and protective effectiveness of three XBB vaccines in older adults 12 months after booster

analysis.research_question_and_background: The study aimed to evaluate the persistence and protective effectiveness of three XBB vaccines in older adults 12 months after booster vaccination, as older adults remain at high risk for severe outcomes due to immunosenescence and waning immunity.
analysis.study_design_and_population: This study is an extended follow-up of a prospective cohort of 90 older adults (≥ 65 years) who received booster vaccinations with trivalent (Tri-XBB.1.5), bivalent (Bi-Omi-XBB), or tetravalent (Tetra-XBB.1) protein vaccines.
analysis.methods: Neutralizing antibody levels were measured using a standardized assay, and protective effectiveness was assessed by comparing infection rates across the three vaccine cohorts over the 12-month period post-booster.
analysis.main_results: At 12 months post-booster, all participants maintained detectable neutralizing antibodies across the three vaccine cohorts, with comparable geometric mean titers (GMTs, all p > 0.05). Significant declines were observed for all variants except D614G, with GMT reductions of 1.7-fold for BA.5, 1.3-fold for XBB.1.5, 1.6-fold for JN.1, 1.2-fold for KP.3, and 1.9-fold for XEC.
analysis.interpretation_and_novelty: The authors interpreted the findings as indicating sustained neutralizing antibody levels across all vaccine cohorts, highlighting the potential for long-term protection against SARS-CoV-2 infection in older adults.
analysis.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: The findings provide important insights into the long-term effectiveness of XBB vaccines in older adults, informing booster strategies and vaccine development for sustained immunity.
analysis.limitations_and_evidence_strength: The study is limited to an abstract-only analysis, and the evidence is based on a single cohort, which may affect generalizability. The evidence strength is moderate due to the lack of detailed statistical analysis and follow-up data.

analysis.summary_en: This study evaluates the persistence and protective effectiveness of three XBB vaccines in older adults 12 months after booster vaccination. The research is motivated by the high risk of severe outcomes in this population due to immunosenescence and waning immunity. The study follows a cohort of 90 older adults who received trivalent, bivalent, or tetravalent protein vaccines. Neutralizing antibody levels were measured using an assay, and protective effectiveness was assessed by comparing infection rates across the vaccine groups. Results show that all participants maintained detectable neutralizing antibodies, with comparable geometric mean titers (GMTs) across the cohorts. However, significant declines were observed for most variants, except D614G. The authors suggest that these findings indicate sustained protection against SARS-CoV-2 infection in older adults. The study has moderate evidence strength due to its abstract-only nature and reliance on a single cohort, which may limit generalizability.

elements_zh.research_question_and_background: 本研究旨在评估三种XBB 疫苗在加强接种12个月后对老年人的持续性和保护效果,因为老年人由于免疫衰老和免疫力下降仍面临严重后果的高风险。
elements_zh.study_design_and_population: 本研究是对一项前瞻性队列研究的扩展随访,该队列研究包括90名老年人(≥65岁),他们接受了三价(Tri-XBB.1.5)、二价(Bi-Omi-XBB)或四价(Tetra-XBB.1)蛋白疫苗的加强接种。
elements_zh.methods: 通过标准化检测方法测量中和抗体水平,并通过比较接种后12个月内三种疫苗 队列研究的感染率来评估保护效果。
elements_zh.main_results: 在加强接种12个月后,所有参与者均保持对三种疫苗 队列研究的可检测中和抗体,几何平均滴度(GMTs,所有p > 0.05)相当。所有变体(除D614G外)均观察到显著下降,其中BA.5的GMT下降了1.7倍,XBB.1.5下降了1.3倍,JN.1下降了1.6倍,KP.3下降了1.2倍,XEC下降了1.9倍。
elements_zh.interpretation_and_novelty: 作者将这些发现解释为所有疫苗 队列研究中和抗体水平的持续性,强调了在老年人中对严重急性呼吸综合征冠状病毒2感染提供长期保护的潜力。
elements_zh.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: 这些发现为了解XBB 疫苗在老年人中的长期有效性提供了重要见解,有助于制定加强接种策略和疫苗开发,以维持长期免疫力。
elements_zh.limitations_and_evidence_strength: 本研究仅限于摘要分析,证据基于单一队列研究,这可能影响其普遍性。由于缺乏详细的统计分析和随访数据,证据强度中等。

papers.title: Avascular necrosis of the femur following COVID-19: an updated systematic review
papers.abstract: BACKGROUND: One of the complications of COVID-19 infection is avascular necrosis of the femoral head. To date, various studies have reported a wide range of osteonecrosis of the femoral head in patients with COVID-19. The previous systematic review included only 14 studies. So, this systematic review aims to update the findings of these studies. METHODS: Databases such as PubMed, Scopus, EMBASE, PsycINFO, Web of Science, and Google Scholar were systematically searched by two independent researchers on April 1st, 2024. RESULTS: A literature search revealed 1229 records, 161 full-texts were evaluated, and finally, 55 studies remained for systematic review. Fifty-five studies were included in this systematic review. Four studies were cross-sectional studies, six were retrospective studies, and the remaining (45studies) were case reports or case-series studies. Totally, 864 cases were included. Except for 12 studies, 43 studies reported the administration of steroid therapy in included cases. The most common underlying conditions were hypertension, followed by diabetes. In 274 (31.7%) of included cases, AVN was bilateral, and both hips were involved. In some studies, non-surgical treatments-including supplement therapy, anticoagulant therapy, physiotherapy, and hyperbaric oxygen therapy-were administered. Several studies reported symptomatic improvement in patients treated with the core decompression approach. Total hip arthroplasty (THA) was the most commonly used surgical treatment. CONCLUSIONS: Avascular necrosis of the femoral head in cases that have survived COVID-19 should be considered carefully as early diagnosis helps to preserve the joint and its function.
papers.journal: Archives of Orthopaedic and Trauma Surgery

analysis.summary_en: This systematic review updates the understanding of avascular necrosis of the femoral head (AVN) as a complication of COVID-19. The review included 55 studies, with 43 reporting steroid therapy use and 43 noting non-surgical treatments such as supplement therapy, anticoagulant therapy, physiotherapy, and hyperbaric oxygen therapy. papers.title: Bloodstream Isolation of Klebsiella Pneumoniae in Adults Hospitalized with SARS-CoV-2 During the Omicron BA.5 Wave: A Retrospective Cohort Study
papers.abstract: Background and Objectives: Secondary bloodstream infection in patients hospitalized with coronavirus disease 2019 (COVID-19) can lengthen admission and increase antimicrobial exposure, yet pathogen-specific evidence from the Omicron period is scarce. We examined how often Klebsiella pneumoniae was recovered from blood among adults admitted with SARS-CoV-2 (severe acute respiratory syndrome coronavirus 2) infection during the Omicron BA.5 wave, and which clinical features and outcomes accompanied it. Materials and Methods: This retrospective single-center cohort comprised 395 adults admitted in Timișoara, Romania, from 12 July to 25 September 2022. pneumoniae in blood culture were compared with all remaining patients, whether their cultures showed no growth or another pathogen. Groups were compared with the Mann–Whitney U and Fisher’s exact tests. The association between K. pneumoniae and a hospital stay of at least 14 days was estimated with Firth penalized logistic regression, adjusted for age, sex, and admission oxygen saturation. Results: Blood cultures grew K. pneumoniae in 16 patients (4.1%), another pathogen in 73 (18.5%), and nothing in 306 (77.5%). Median length of stay was 17.5 days (IQR (interquartile range) 9.8–25.2) with K. pneumoniae and 9.0 days (IQR 7.0–16.0) in the rest of the cohort (p = 0.006); a stay of at least 14 days occurred in 56.3% versus 28.0% (unadjusted OR 3.31, p = 0.022). The association persisted after adjustment (Firth adjusted OR 3.18, 95% CI 1.14–8.87; p = 0.027; maximum-likelihood estimate 3.25, 95% CI 1.16–9.12; p = 0.025). In-hospital death occurred in 1 of 16 exposed patients (6.3%) and in 61 of 379 others (16.1%; Fisher’s exact p = 0.485); with a single exposed death, the age- and sex-adjusted Firth estimate was imprecise (adjusted OR 0.48, 95% CI 0.04–2.21). pneumoniae bloodstream isolation was infrequent in this Omicron BA.5 cohort but was accompanied by a markedly longer hospital stay. Causality and an effect on mortality cannot be inferred: culture dates, place of acquisition, device exposure, and isolate susceptibility were not available, the untimed exposure is prone to immortal-time bias, and no non-COVID-19 comparator was studied. Prospective surveillance combining time-stamped microbiology with resistance phenotyping is needed.

analysis.methods: The study used Firth penalized logistic regression to estimate the association between K. pneumoniae and a hospital stay of at least 14 days, adjusting for age, sex, and admission oxygen saturation. Statistical comparisons were made using Mann–Whitney U and Fisher’s exact tests.

analysis.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: The findings highlight the need for prospective surveillance that integrates time-stamped microbiology data with resistance phenotyping to better understand the clinical implications of K. pneumoniae bloodstream infections in SARS-CoV-2 patients.

analysis.summary_en: This retrospective cohort study investigated the frequency of Klebsiella pneumoniae bloodstream isolation among adults hospitalized with SARS-CoV-2 during the Omicron BA.5 wave in Romania. The study found that K. pneumoniae was isolated in 4.1% of patients, with a significantly longer hospital stay compared to those without bloodstream infection. The association between K. pneumoniae and prolonged hospitalization remained significant after adjustment for age, sex, and admission oxygen saturation. However, causality and mortality effects could not be inferred due to the lack of detailed microbiology data and the absence of a non-COVID-19 comparator. The study underscores the need for prospective surveillance to better understand the clinical impact of K. pneumoniae in SARS-CoV-2 patients. The evidence is moderate due to the observational design and missing data.

elements_zh.research_question_and_background: 本研究旨在探讨在奥密克戎BA.5波浪期间,因严重急性呼吸综合征冠状病毒2住院的成人中肺炎克雷伯菌血流分离的频率及其与临床特征和结果的关联。
elements_zh.study_design_and_population: 在罗马尼亚蒂米什瓦拉医院进行了一项回顾性单中心队列研究,涉及2022年7月12日至9月25日因严重急性呼吸综合征冠状病毒2感染住院的395名成人。
elements_zh.methods: 研究使用Firth惩罚逻辑回归来估计肺炎克雷伯菌与住院时间至少14天的关联,并调整了年龄、性别和入院时的血氧饱和度。使用Mann–Whitney U检验和Fisher精确检验进行统计比较。
elements_zh.main_results: 肺炎克雷伯菌在16名患者(4.1%)的血液培养中被分离,73名患者(18.5%)分离出其他病原体,306名患者(77.5%)未分离出任何病原体。肺炎克雷伯菌组的中位住院时间为17.5天(IQR 9.8–25.2),而其余队列患者的中位住院时间为9.0天(IQR 7.0–16.0)。住院时间至少14天的未调整比值比为3.31(p = 0.022)。

analysis_en.research_question_and_background: The study aimed to investigate the frequency of Klebsiella pneumoniae bloodstream isolation among adults hospitalized with SARS-CoV-2 during the Omicron BA.5 wave and its association with clinical features and outcomes.
analysis_en.study_design_and_population: A retrospective single-center cohort study was conducted at a hospital in Timișoara, Romania, involving 395 adults admitted with SARS-CoV-2 infection from 12 July to 25 September 2022.
analysis_en.methods: The study used Firth penalized logistic regression to estimate the association between K. pneumoniae and a hospital stay of at least 14 days, adjusting for age, sex, and admission oxygen saturation. Statistical comparisons were made using Mann–Whitney U and Fisher’s exact tests.
analysis_en.main_results: pneumoniae was isolated from blood cultures in 16 patients (4.1%), another pathogen in 73 (18.5%), and nothing in 306 (77.5%). pneumoniae had a median hospital stay of 17.5 days (IQR 9.8–25.2) compared to 9.0 days (IQR 7.0–16.0) in the rest of the cohort. The unadjusted odds ratio for a stay of at least 14 days was 3.31 (p = 0.022).
analysis_en.interpretation_and_novelty: The association between K. pneumoniae and prolonged hospital stays remained significant after adjustment, suggesting a potential clinical impact, although causality could not be established due to the observational nature of the study.
analysis_en.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: The findings highlight the need for prospective surveillance that integrates time-stamped microbiology data with resistance phenotyping to better understand the clinical implications of K. pneumoniae bloodstream infections in SARS-CoV-2 patients.
analysis_en.limitations_and_evidence_strength: The study is limited by its retrospective design, lack of culture dates, place of acquisition, device exposure, and isolate susceptibility data, and the absence of a non-COVID-19 comparator. The evidence is moderate due to these limitations.

papers.title_zh: Bloodstream Isolation of Klebsiella Pneumoniae in Adults Hospitalized with SARS-CoV-2 During the Omicron BA.5 Wave: A Retrospective Cohort Study
papers.source_body_en: Background and Objectives: Secondary bloodstream infection in patients hospitalized with coronavirus disease 2019 (COVID-19) can lengthen admission and increase antimicrobial exposure, yet pathogen-specific evidence from the Omicron period is scarce. We examined how often Klebsiella pneumoniae was recovered from blood among adults admitted with SARS-CoV-2 (severe acute respiratory syndrome coronavirus 2) infection during the Omicron BA.5 wave, and which clinical features and outcomes accompanied it. Materials and Methods: This retrospective single-center cohort comprised 395 adults admitted in Timișoara, Romania, from 12 July to 25 September 2022. pneumoniae in blood culture were compared with all remaining patients, whether their cultures showed no growth or another pathogen. Groups were compared with the Mann–Whitney U and Fisher’s exact tests. The association between K. pneumoniae and a hospital stay of at least 14 days was estimated with Firth penalized logistic regression, adjusted for age, sex, and admission oxygen saturation. Results: Blood cultures grew K. pneumoniae in 16 patients (4.1%), another pathogen in 73 (18.5%), and nothing in 306 (77.5%). Median length of stay was 17.5 days (IQR (interquartile range) 9.8–25.2) with K. pneumoniae and 9.0 days (IQR 7.0–16.0) in the rest of the cohort (p = 0.006); a stay of at least 14 days occurred in 56.3% versus 28.0% (unadjusted OR 3.31, p = 0.022). The association persisted after adjustment (Firth adjusted OR 3.18, 95% CI 1.14–8.87; p = 0.027; maximum-likelihood estimate 3.25, 95% CI 1.16–9.12; p = 0.025). In-hospital death occurred in 1 of 16 exposed patients (6.3%) and in 61 of 379 others (16.1%; Fisher’s exact p = 0.485); with a single exposed death, the age- and sex-adjusted Firth estimate was imprecise (adjusted OR 0.48, 95% CI 0.04–2.21). pneumoniae bloodstream isolation was infrequent in this Omicron BA.5 cohort but was accompanied by a markedly longer hospital stay. Causality and an effect on mortality cannot be inferred: culture dates, place of acquisition, device exposure, and isolate susceptibility were not available, the untimed exposure is prone to immortal-time bias, and no non-COVID-19 comparator was studied. Prospective surveillance combining time-stamped microbiology with resistance phenotyping is needed.

papers.title: Letter to the Editor: Coronavirus disease 2019, multisystem inflammatory syndrome, and children’s hearts: Finding answers with cardiac magnetic resonance imaging
papers.abstract: The article refers to “Persistent long-term subclinical myocardial changes in multisystem inflammatory syndrome in children revealed by cardiac magnetic resonance and galectin-3” by OV et al published in the World Journal of Clinical Pediatrics , multisystem inflammatory syndrome in children (MIS-C) associated with coronavirus disease 2019 (COVID-19) and its cardiovascular complications. MIS-C frequently causes cardiovascular complications, including coronary artery dilatation, low left ventricular (LV) ejection fraction, diastolic dysfunction, myocarditis, and pericardial effusion, decreases over time, usually resolving within 6-9 months after the disease onset. Echocardiographic evaluations reveal mild to moderate LV dysfunction, resolving within two weeks. Severe dysfunction normalizes after approximately 1.5 months. Global longitudinal strain proves valuable for detecting subclinical myocardial damage. Long-term effects based on cardiac magnetic resonance imaging (CMRI) data indicate the persistent myocardial edema and/or fibrosisupto12 months after the initialevent. Signs of interstitial fibrosis were found in 7.7% of patients during a one-year follow-up period. CMRI is an important additional method in the assessment of children who have experienced multisystem inflammatory syndrome in COVID-19, especially in patients with persistent symptoms or abnormal data from other cardiac findings.

MIS-C frequently causes cardiovascular complications, including coronary artery dilatation, low left ventricular (LV) ejection fraction, diastolic dysfunction, myocarditis, and pericardial effusion, decreases over time, usually resolving within 6-9 months after the disease onset. Echocardiographic evaluations reveal mild to moderate LV dysfunction, resolving within two weeks. Severe dysfunction normalizes after approximately 1.5 months. Global longitudinal strain proves valuable for detecting subclinical myocardial damage. Long-term effects based on cardiac magnetic resonance imaging (CMRI) data indicate the persistent myocardial edema and/or fibrosisupto12 months after the initialevent. Signs of interstitial fibrosis were found in 7.7% of patients during a one-year follow-up period. CMRI is an important additional method in the assessment of children who have experienced multisystem inflammatory syndrome in COVID-19, especially in patients with persistent symptoms or abnormal data from other cardiac findings.

analysis.research_question_and_background: The study aimed to investigate the cardiovascular complications of multisystem inflammatory syndrome in children (MIS-C) associated with coronavirus disease 2019 (COVID-19) and its long-term effects on cardiac health.
analysis.study_design_and_population: The study focused on children who had experienced MIS-C linked to COVID-19, examining their cardiovascular complications and long-term cardiac outcomes through follow-up assessments.
analysis.methods: Cardiac magnetic resonance imaging (CMRI) and galectin-3 measurements were used to assess myocardial changes, while echocardiographic evaluations were conducted to monitor left ventricular (LV) function.
analysis.main_results: Persistent myocardial edema and/or fibrosis were observed in some patients up to 12 months after the initial event, and signs of interstitial fibrosis were found in 7.7% of patients during a one-year follow-up period.
analysis.interpretation_and_novelty: The findings highlight the potential for long-term cardiac damage in children with MIS-C, emphasizing the importance of CMRI in detecting subclinical myocardial changes.
analysis.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: These results suggest that CMRI should be considered for assessing long-term cardiac effects in children with MIS-C, particularly those with persistent symptoms or abnormal findings from other cardiac tests.
analysis.limitations_and_evidence_strength: The study is limited by its observational nature and potential for bias, but the evidence is supported by CMRI data and follow-up assessments, providing moderate confidence in the findings.

analysis.summary_en: This study investigates the cardiovascular complications of multisystem inflammatory syndrome in children (MIS-C) associated with coronavirus disease 2019 (COVID-19) and its long-term effects on cardiac health. Using cardiac magnetic resonance imaging (CMRI) and galectin-3 measurements, the research reveals persistent myocardial edema and fibrosis in some patients up to 12 months post-onset, with interstitial fibrosis observed in 7.7% during a one-year follow-up. The findings suggest that CMRI is valuable for detecting subclinical myocardial damage in children with MIS-C, especially those with ongoing symptoms or abnormal cardiac findings. However, the study's observational design and potential for bias limit the confidence in its conclusions, though the evidence is supported by CMRI data and follow-up assessments, offering moderate confidence in the results.

elements_zh.research_question_and_background: The study aimed to investigate the cardiovascular complications of multisystem inflammatory syndrome in children (MIS-C) associated with coronavirus disease 2019 (COVID-19) and its long-term effects on cardiac health.
elements_zh.study_design_and_population: The study focused on children who had experienced MIS-C linked to COVID-19, examining their cardiovascular complications and long-term cardiac outcomes through follow-up assessments.
elements_zh.methods: 使用心脏磁共振成像(CMRI)和半乳糖凝集素-3测量来评估心肌变化,同时通过超声心动图评估来监测左心室(LV)功能。
elements_zh.main_results: 一些患者在初始事件后12个月内仍观察到持续的心肌水肿和/或纤维化,一年随访期间,7.7%的患者出现了间质性纤维化的迹象。
elements_zh.interpretation_and_novelty: 研究结果突显了多系统炎症综合征在儿童中可能存在的长期心脏损伤风险,强调了心脏磁共振成像(CMRI)在检测亚临床心肌变化中的重要性。
elements_zh.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: 这些结果表明,对于患有MIS-C且有持续症状或其它心脏检查异常发现的儿童,应考虑使用CMRI评估长期心脏效应。
elements_zh.limitations_and_evidence_strength: 本研究的局限性在于其观察性质和潜在的偏倚,但研究结果得到了心脏磁共振成像数据和随访评估的支持,为研究发现提供了中等程度的可信度。

papers.title: A Pilot Surveillance Program to Identify Emerging SARS-CoV-2 Variants in International Travelers Arriving at a Major International Airport: Prospective Cohort Evaluation
papers.abstract: Background: Testing arriving international travelers for COVID-19 paired with whole-genome sequencing (WGS) may identify new introductions of SARS-CoV-2 variants of concern in California, enabling a timely public health response. Traveler genomic surveillance may be a way to improve gaps in worldwide disease genomic surveillance. Objective: This paper aimed to describe a pilot surveillance program to identify SARS-CoV-2 variants in arriving international travelers at San Francisco International Airport (SFO). Methods: The California Department of Public Health implemented a pilot program at SFO to voluntarily test arriving international travelers for COVID-19 from June 2021 to November 2021 to identify SARS-CoV-2 variants. Arriving international travelers were offered self-collect COVID-19 antigen tests upon arrival at SFO. Travelers with positive COVID-19 antigen tests or with COVID-19 symptoms were recommended to self-collect and mail an additional specimen for diagnostic molecular testing. WGS of SARS-CoV-2 was performed on RNA extracts from positive tests to identify variants. Results: In total, 2.1% (19,008/892,558) of all arriving international travelers at SFO from 133 different countries of departure enrolled in the program. The COVID-19 test positivity among this group was 0.7% (33/5038), and the weekly test positivity range, 0% to 1.5%, was lower than the weekly test positivity across the state of California during the same time frame. Arriving international travelers departing from Turkey (3/145, 2.1%), Mexico (7/602, 1.2%), and the United Kingdom (6/626, 1.0%) had the highest test positivity. Of the 14 positive molecular tests, 10 (71.4%) were sequenced, and all were found to belong to the SARS-CoV-2 Delta B.1.617.2 lineage, the most prevalent SARS-CoV-2 variant in California and worldwide at the time. Conclusions: Voluntary testing of arriving international travelers paired with WGS was operationally and logistically feasible. Although the number of sequenced positive COVID-19 specimens in this program was limited, the lessons learned from this pilot informed improvements to subsequent iterations of traveler viral genomic surveillance in California and highlighted the potential value of traveler viral genomic surveillance to support early identification and characterization of emerging infectious diseases entering a region.

papers.title: Cryptic spread of SARS-CoV-2 undermined targeted travel restrictions
papers.abstract: Abstract The effectiveness of travel restrictions in mitigating the spread of novel viral variants remains understudied, particularly in regions with sparse genomic surveillance. We evaluated the efficacy of these restrictions in Western Asia, where countries sequenced less than one percent of SARS-CoV-2 cases in 2021, focusing on Iraq’s travel ban on India and the tourist travel restriction. We generated 535 SARS-CoV-2 whole-genome sequences from clinical samples collected in Duhok, Iraq, between June 2021 and March 2022, encompassing the Delta and Omicron variant waves. Using discrete Bayesian phylogeographic modeling, we reconstructed spatiotemporal viral spread patterns to determine whether travel restrictions delayed the introduction of the variants into the country, postponed community transmission onset, or altered the geographic sources of viral introductions over time. We found that the Delta variant was introduced into Iraq three months before the targeted travel ban was enacted, predominantly from Western and Southern Asia, whereas the Omicron variant was introduced despite the tourist travel restriction already being in place. We also show that both variants had established community transmission within the country despite travel restrictions, rendering these measures ineffective. Analysis of travel restrictions on a global scale reveals similar patterns of limited efficacy in mitigating the introductions of novel SARS-CoV-2 variants, challenging the usefulness of such measures.

analysis.research_question_and_background: The study aimed to evaluate the efficacy of travel restrictions in mitigating the spread of SARS-CoV-2 variants, particularly in regions with sparse genomic surveillance, addressing the understudied nature of such measures.
analysis.study_design_and_population: The study evaluated the impact of travel restrictions on SARS-CoV-2 variants in Western Asia, focusing on Iraq’s travel ban on India and tourist travel restriction, using 535 SARS-CoV-2 whole-genome sequences from clinical samples collected in Duhok, Iraq, between June 2021 and March 2022.
analysis.methods: The researchers generated 535 SARS-CoV-2 whole-genome sequences and used discrete Bayesian phylogeographic modeling to reconstruct spatiotemporal viral spread patterns, determining the introduction and transmission of Delta and Omicron variants despite travel restrictions.
analysis.main_results: The study found that the Delta variant was introduced into Iraq three months before the travel ban, predominantly from Western and Southern Asia, and the Omicron variant was introduced despite the tourist travel restriction already being in place, both variants establishing community transmission within the country.
analysis.interpretation_and_novelty: The findings suggest that travel restrictions are ineffective in mitigating the introduction of SARS-CoV-2 variants, challenging the usefulness of such measures globally.
analysis.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: The study’s findings caution against relying on travel restrictions as a primary strategy for mitigating the spread of SARS-CoV-2 variants, emphasizing the need for more comprehensive surveillance and control measures.
analysis.limitations_and_evidence_strength: The study’s limitations include the reliance on genomic surveillance data from a single region, which may not be representative of other areas, and the potential for confounding factors in the analysis.

analysis.summary_en: This study evaluated the effectiveness of travel restrictions in mitigating the spread of SARS-CoV-2 variants in Western Asia, particularly in Iraq. Despite targeted measures, the Delta and Omicron variants were introduced into the country, establishing community transmission, suggesting that travel restrictions are insufficient for variant control.

elements_zh.research_question_and_background: 本研究旨在评估旅行限制在遏制严重急性呼吸综合征冠状病毒2变异株传播方面的有效性,特别是在基因组监测病例稀少的地区,以解决此类措施研究不足的问题。
elements_zh.study_design_and_population: 本研究评估了旅行限制对西亚地区严重急性呼吸综合征冠状病毒2变异株的影响,重点关注伊拉克对印度实施的旅行禁令和旅游旅行限制,使用了从2021年6月至2022年3月在伊拉克杜胡克收集的临床样本中生成的535个严重急性呼吸综合征冠状病毒2全基因组序列。
elements_zh.methods: 研究人员生成了535个严重急性呼吸综合征冠状病毒2全基因组序列,并利用离散贝叶斯系统发育地理建模重建了病毒的时空传播模式,以确定在旅行限制下Delta和Omicron变异株的引入和传播情况。
elements_zh.main_results: 研究发现,Delta变异株在旅行禁令实施前三个月已进入伊拉克,主要来自西亚和南亚,而Omicron变异株则在旅游旅行限制已实施的情况下仍被引入,这两种变异株均在该国建立了社区传播。
elements_zh.interpretation_and_novelty: 这些发现表明,旅行限制在遏制严重急性呼吸综合征冠状病毒2变异株的引入方面是无效的,挑战了此类措施在全球范围内的实用性。
elements_zh.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: 本研究的发现警示人们不要依赖旅行限制作为遏制严重急性呼吸综合征冠状病毒2变异株传播的主要策略,强调需要更全面的监测和控制措施。
elements_zh.limitations_and_evidence_strength: 本研究的局限性包括依赖单一地区的基因组监测数据,这可能无法代表其他地区的情况,以及分析中可能存在混杂因素。

analysis_en.research_question_and_background: The study aimed to evaluate the efficacy of travel restrictions in mitigating the spread of SARS-CoV-2 variants, particularly in regions with sparse genomic surveillance, addressing the understudied nature of such measures.
analysis_en.study_design_and_population: The study evaluated the impact of travel restrictions on SARS-CoV-2 variants in Western Asia, focusing on Iraq’s travel ban on India and tourist travel restriction, using 535 SARS-CoV-2 whole-genome sequences from clinical samples collected in Duhok, Iraq, between June 2021 and March 2022.
analysis_en.methods: The researchers generated 535 SARS-CoV-2 whole-genome sequences and used discrete Bayesian phylogeographic modeling to reconstruct spatiotemporal viral spread patterns, determining the introduction and transmission of Delta and Omicron variants despite travel restrictions.
analysis_en.main_results: The study found that the Delta variant was introduced into Iraq three months before the travel ban, predominantly from Western and Southern Asia, and the Omicron variant was introduced despite the tourist travel restriction already being in place, both variants establishing community transmission within the country.
analysis_en.interpretation_and_novelty: The findings suggest that travel restrictions are ineffective in mitigating the introduction of SARS-CoV-2 variants, challenging the usefulness of such measures globally.
analysis_en.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: The study’s findings caution against relying on travel restrictions as a primary strategy for mitigating the spread of SARS-CoV-2 variants, emphasizing the need for more comprehensive surveillance and control measures.
analysis_en.limitations_and_evidence_strength: The study’s limitations include the reliance on genomic surveillance data from a single region, which may not be representative of other areas, and the potential for confounding factors in the analysis.

papers.title_zh: 严重急性呼吸综合征冠状病毒2隐秘传播削弱了针对性旅行限制的有效性
papers.source_body_en: Abstract The effectiveness of travel restrictions in mitigating the spread of novel viral variants remains understudied, particularly in regions with sparse genomic surveillance. We evaluated the efficacy of these restrictions in Western Asia, where countries sequenced less than one percent of SARS-CoV-2 cases in 2021, focusing on Iraq’s travel ban on India and the tourist travel restriction. We generated 535 SARS-CoV-2 whole-genome sequences from clinical samples collected in Duhok, Iraq, between June 2021 and March 2022, encompassing the Delta and Omicron variant waves. Using discrete Bayesian phylogeographic modeling, we reconstructed spatiotemporal viral spread patterns to determine whether travel restrictions delayed the introduction of the variants into the country, postponed community transmission onset, or altered the geographic sources of viral introductions over time. We found that the Delta variant was introduced into Iraq three months before the targeted travel ban was enacted, predominantly from Western and Southern Asia, whereas the Omicron variant was introduced despite the tourist travel restriction already being in place. We also show that both variants had established community transmission within the country despite travel restrictions, rendering these measures ineffective. Analysis of travel restrictions on a global scale reveals similar patterns of limited efficacy in mitigating the introductions of novel SARS-CoV-2 variants, challenging the usefulness of such measures.
papers.abstract_zh: 摘要 旅行限制在遏制新型病毒变异株传播方面的有效性尚未得到充分研究,尤其是在基因组监测病例稀少的地区。我们评估了这些限制在西亚的影响,其中2021年各国对严重急性呼吸综合征冠状病毒2病例的基因组测序率低于1%,重点关注伊拉克对印度实施的旅行禁令和旅游旅行限制。我们从2021年6月至2022年3月在伊拉克杜胡克收集的临床样本中生成了535个严重急性呼吸综合征冠状病毒2全基因组序列,涵盖了Delta和Omicron变异株的传播浪潮。利用离散贝叶斯系统发育地理建模,我们重建了病毒的时空传播模式,以确定旅行限制是否延迟了变异株进入该国,推迟了社区传播的开始,或是否改变了病毒引入的地理来源随时间的变化。我们发现,Delta变异株在旅行禁令实施前三个月已进入伊拉克,主要来自西亚和南亚,而Omicron变异株则在旅游旅行限制已实施的情况下仍被引入。我们还表明,尽管有旅行限制,这两种变异株已在该国建立了社区传播,使这些措施无效。对全球旅行限制的分析显示,这些措施在遏制新型严重急性呼吸综合征冠状病毒2变异株引入方面的效果有限,挑战了此类措施的实用性。

papers.title: P-462: Increased incidence of diabetic ketoacidosis (DKA) during COVID-19 pandemic
papers.abstract: Abstract Introduction The COVID-19 pandemic led to strict measures and healthcare shifts, delaying diagnosis of conditions like type 1 diabetes (T1D). In children, this increased DKA at diagnosis, often more severe, likely due to reduced access to care and fear of infection during the pandemic. Objectives To compare the severity and frequency of DKA in new-onset type 1 diabetes mellitus patients and in patients with previous diagnosis of T1D in a referral Pediatric hospital during and before the COVID-19 pandemic. Methods This retrospective cohort study reviewed medical records of children with DKA at a referral Pediatric hospital between April/2018 and December/2019 (pre-pandemic period) and between April/2020 and December/2021 (pandemic period). We analyzed demographics, clinical features, hospital stay, and laboratory data, excluding incomplete records. The means, percentages, and variability were calculated, and the chi-squared test and Fisher’s exact test were applied accordingly. Results We analyzed 55 patients with 74 DKA admissions, comparing pre-pandemic (Group 1) and pandemic (Group 2) periods. The Gender distribution shifted toward females. Age and diagnosis patterns showed trends but no significant differences. Table 1 shows the characteristics of Group 1 and 2. Conclusions Our study found a 39% rise in patients and 85% in admissions, There were a marked increase in DKA cases during the pandemic period, consistent with international data, but without differences in severity, though with a trend toward more ventilation and dialysis. Most cases were moderate to severe, reflecting delayed diagnosis.

analysis.summary_en: This study investigates the impact of the COVID-19 pandemic on the incidence and severity of diabetic ketoacidosis (DKA) in children with type 1 diabetes (T1D). It compares data from pre-pandemic (April 2018–December 2019) and pandemic (April 2020–December 2021) periods at a referral Pediatric hospital. The results show a 39% increase in patients and 85% rise in DKA admissions during the pandemic, with a trend toward more ventilation and dialysis. However, no significant differences in severity were observed. The study underscores the need for improved surveillance and early diagnosis of T1D in children during public health crises, as delayed diagnosis may contribute to more severe DKA cases.

elements_zh.evidence_base_and_review_method: 本研究为回顾性分析,审查了2018年4月至2019年12月(疫情前)和2020年4月至2021年12月(疫情期间)期间在一家转诊儿科医院就诊的儿童DKA病例的医疗记录。分析包括人口学特征、临床表现、住院时间和实验室数据,排除不完整的记录。计算了均值、百分比和变异情况,并相应应用了卡方检验和费舍尔精确检验。
elements_zh.consensus_and_key_conclusions: 本研究发现,疫情期间患者数量增加了39%,DKA入院数量增加了85%。DKA病例数量显著增加,与国际数据一致,但未观察到严重程度的差异,尽管有向更多需要通气和透析的趋势。
elements_zh.controversies_and_evidence_gaps: 本研究未报告严重程度的显著差异,尽管有向更多需要通气和透析的趋势。年龄和诊断模式显示出趋势,但无显著差异。证据未提供关于DKA病例增加机制或诊断延迟长期影响的详细信息。
elements_zh.research_and_practice_implications: 研究结果表明,在疫情期间需要改善对儿童类型1糖尿病的诊断和早期干预。这些发现强调了保持医疗服务可及性以及监测类型1糖尿病延迟诊断的重要性,因为这可能导致更严重的DKA病例。

papers.title: Dysfunctional neutrophil response in COVID-19 infection varies by subtype.
papers.abstract: The SARS-CoV-2 virus significantly evolved, with several new strains being identified. Transmissibility has increased with each strain, corresponding with a decrease in mortality. We previously demonstrated novel dysfunctional neutrophil responses in patients with the Alpha variant of COVID-19 compared with control patients with community-acquired pneumonia. We investigated if strain variation altered neutrophil dysfunction we had previously observed. Patients with COVID-19 not requiring intensive care were recruited between January 2021 and May 2022 from the Queen Elizabeth Hospital Birmingham; 41 patients had the Alpha variant, 32 had the Delta variant, and 14 had the Omicron variant. Neutrophils isolated from whole blood were investigated for phagocytosis of labelled Streptococcus pneumoniae, Transwell migration toward IL-8, neutrophil extracellular (NET) formation, and surface phenotype. Neutrophil phagocytosis was significantly increased in the Delta variant (vs Alpha, P = 0.0012; vs Omicron P = 0.0209). Transwell migration was also significantly reduced in patients with the Omicron variant (vs Alpha P = 0.0002; vs Delta, P = 0.0129). There was a significant reduction in NET formation from patients with Omicron (vs Alpha, P = 0.0031; vs Delta, P = 0.0231). Compared with patients with Alpha, neutrophils from those with Omicron had reduced expression of CD10 (P = 0.0004), CD54 (P = 0.0015), CD62L (P = 0.0013), and CD11c (P < 0.0001). CXCR2 expression was higher in neutrophils from patients with the Omicron variant compared with those with Alpha (P = 0.0001). Neutrophil function and phenotype differ among the variants of COVID-19 infection in hospitalized patients. Neutrophil changes suggest more accurate migration in patients with the Omicron variant, leading to decreased neutrophil host-mediated tissue damage. This may contribute to the overall milder clinical Omicron phenotype. Ongoing research and review of therapies remain important as the virus evolves.

analysis.summary_en: This study investigated whether strain variation of SARS-CoV-2 altered neutrophil dysfunction previously observed in patients with the Alpha variant. The research focused on patients with non-intensive care COVID-19 infections recruited from the Queen Elizabeth Hospital Birmingham between 2021 and 2022. Neutrophil function was assessed through phagocytosis, migration, NET formation, and surface phenotype. Results showed increased phagocytosis in Delta variant patients, reduced migration in Omicron variant patients, decreased NET formation in Omicron patients, and altered surface marker expression. The findings suggest that neutrophil changes in Omicron may lead to reduced host-mediated tissue damage, potentially explaining its milder clinical phenotype. The study provides insights into variant-specific immune responses but does not address its limitations.

news.excerpt_original: National flu and COVID-19 surveillance report: 5 November 2026 (week 45) GOV.UK
news.priority_tier_reason: 政府、WHO/CDC/ECDC或其他官方公共卫生来源
news.content_title: National flu and COVID-19 surveillance report: 5 November 2026 (week 45)
news.content: This publication is licensed under the terms of the Open Government Licence v3.0 except where otherwise stated. To view this licence, visit nationalarchives.gov.uk/doc/open-government-licence/version/3 or write to the Information Policy Team, The National Archives, Kew, London TW9 4DU, or email: psi@nationalarchives.gov.uk . Where we have identified any third party copyright information you will need to obtain permission from the copyright holders concerned. This publication is available at https://www.gov.uk/government/statistics/national-flu-and-covid-19-surveillance-reports-2026-to-2027-season/national-flu-and-covid-19-surveillance-report-5-november-2026-week-45 This report summarises the information from the surveillance systems which are used to monitor COVID-19 (caused by severe acute respiratory syndrome coronavirus 2 (SARS-CoV-2)), influenza, respiratory syncytial virus ( RSV ) and diseases caused by other seasonal respiratory viruses in England. The report is based on data up to week 44 of 2026 (26 October to 1 November 2026). The main messages of this report are: Annual reports for the 2025 to 2026 season: Influenza in the UK, annual epidemiological report: winter 2025 to 2026 (published 28 May 2026) Epidemiology of COVID-19 in England (published 25 June 2026) Seasonal influenza vaccine uptake in all GP patients: annual report 2025 to 2026 (published 28 May 2026) Seasonal influenza vaccine uptake in school-aged children: annual report 2025 to 2026 (published 28 May 2026) Seasonal influenza vaccine uptake in frontline healthcare workers: annual report 2025 to 2026 (published 28 May 2026) Influenza activity showed variable trends across surveillance indicators and is circulating at low levels. Emergency department ( ED ) attendances for influenza-like-illness ( ILI ) increased slightly and were above seasonally expected levels. The number of influenza-confirmed acute respiratory infection ( ARI ) incidents decreased compared with the previous week. A briefing note has been issued to inform the NHS that influenza activity is now above baseline levels. Influenza vaccination data was unavailable or incomplete at the time of analysis in weeks 41 and 42 and led to several cohorts not being published in week 42. This has been corrected since week 43, and all cohorts are included. This will be corrected retrospectively in the report for week 42. There remains an issue that affects the attribution of vaccinations by provider setting. The correct identification of vaccinations administered in pharmacies cannot currently be reliably distinguished from those administered in general practices or other healthcare settings. As a result, some pharmacy vaccinations are likely to be misclassified as general practice or other healthcare settings, artificially increasing vaccination activity reported for general practices and other healthcare settings and reducing activity reported for pharmacies. This is not expected to affect overall vaccination uptake estimates, which are considered to remain an accurate reflection of the influenza vaccination programme. Compared with the equivalent week last season (week 44 data, 2025 to 2026), vaccine uptake is lower among patients aged 65 years and over (59.1% vs 61.5%), patients aged 6 months to under 65 years in clinical risk groups (27.9% vs 28.9%), those aged 2 years (33.3% vs 34.2%), and those aged 3 years (33.1% vs 34.3%). In contrast, vaccine uptake is higher among pregnant women (31.1% vs 29.7%). COVID-19 activity decreased and is circulating at low levels. ED attendances for COVID-19-like illness remained stable. The number of COVID-19 confirmed acute respiratory infections ( ARI ) incidents decreased compared with the previous week. By the end of week 44 2026, 47.7% of all people aged 75 years and over in England had been vaccinated with an autumn 2026 dose. Similarly, 20.5% of all people aged under 75 years with a weakened immune system in England had been vaccinated with an autumn 2026 dose since 1 October 2026. RSV activity increased and is circulating at baseline levels. ED attendances for acute bronchiolitis increased and were within seasonally expected levels. Note 1: these indicators use the moving epidemic method ( MEM ) and the mean standard deviation method ( MSD ) to define thresholds to determine their respective levels of activity. Further information on these methods can be found in Influenza surveillance in Europe: establishing epidemic thresholds by the Moving Epidemic Method and Setting thresholds to determine COVID-19 activity levels using the mean standard deviation ( MSD ) method, England, 2022 to 2024 . The MEM approach is well-established for some influenza surveillance indicators, however, for other indicators both the MEM and MSD are experimental and may be subject to future revision. Influenza laboratory surveillance and GP swabbing positivity have transitioned from using MEM to using MSD . These approaches will be considered alongside expert opinion and triangulation of other data sources. The Second Generation Surveillance System ( SGSS ) captures test result information for notifiable infectious diseases, including COVID-19 and influenza, from laboratories in England. The unified sample dataset ( USD ) stores all SARS-CoV-2 test results reported to SGSS , Respiratory DataMart and UKHSA laboratories, and is used to calculate the percentage of tests positive for SARS-CoV-2 among all SARS-CoV-2 tests conducted. As of 3 November 2026, there were a total of 1,730 COVID-19 cases identified in hospital settings in week 44, decreasing from 2,052 cases in the previous week. SARS-CoV-2 (COVID-19) PCR positivity in hospital settings decreased slightly in week 44, with a rolling 7-day positivity rate of 7.6% up to Sunday 1 November 2026 compared with 8.1% for the same period on the previous Sunday. Positivity rates were highest among those aged 85 years and over with a rolling 7-day positivity rate of 11.1% up to Sunday 1 November 2026. This has remained stable compared to 10.8% in the same age group on the previous Sunday. Note 2: data from previous seasons is aligned by day. Note 3: testing policy and practice may change over time which can impact positivity rates, therefore comparisons over time should be interpreted with caution. Notable changes in testing policy occurred during 2022 to 2023, which are outlined in the data quality report . Note 4: the highlighted line corresponds to the age group in the subplot title, grey lines correspond to all other age groups. Influenza positivity increased in week 44, with a rolling 7-day positivity rate of 7.6% up to Sunday 1 November 2026. This is compared with 6.8% on the previous Sunday. By type, influenza A positivity increased in week 44, with a rolling 7-day positivity rate of 6.8% up to Sunday 1 November 2026. Influenza B positivity remained stable in the same week, with a rolling 7-day positivity rate of 0.3% up to Sunday 1 November 2026. Influenza A positivity rates were highest among those aged between 5 and 11 years, with a rolling 7-day positivity rate of 10.7% up to Sunday 1 November 2026. This has decreased from 15.8% in the same age group on the previous Sunday. Influenza B positivity rates for the same period were highest among those aged between 5 and 11 years, with a rolling 7-day positivity rate of 1.0%. This has decreased from 2.0% in the same age group on the previous Sunday. RSV swab-positivity based PCR test results reported through SGSS have been included as a pilot indicator from week 49 2025 onwards. RSV positivity increased in week 44, with a rolling 7-day positivity rate of 2.5% up to Sunday 1 November 2026, compared with 1.6% up to the previous Sunday. RSV positivity rates were highest in those aged between 0 and 4 years with a rolling 7-day positivity rate of 16.0% up to Sunday 1 November 2026 in week 44. This has increased from 10.0% in the same age group on the previous Sunday. Respiratory DataMart is a sentinel laboratory-based surveillance system where participating laboratories report positive and negative test results for a number of respiratory viruses from samples primarily taken in hospital. A small proportion of primary care samples are also included in this reporting. In week 44, data is based on reporting from 9 out of the 14 sentinel laboratories. In week 44, 4,137 respiratory specimens reported through the Respiratory DataMart System were tested for influenza. There were 307 positive samples for influenza: 221 influenza A (not subtyped), 7 influenza A (H3N2), 72 influenza A (H1N1)pdm09, and 11 influenza B. Overall, influenza positivity increased slightly to 7.4% in week 44 compared with 6.4% in the previous week. In week 44, 4,918 respiratory specimens reported through the Respiratory DataMart System were tested for SARS-CoV-2. There were 367 positive samples for SARS-CoV-2. SARS-CoV-2 positivity remained stable at 7.5% compared with 7.7% in the previous week, with the highest positivity in those aged 80 years and over at 9.9%. RSV positivity increased to 2.9%, with the highest positivity in those aged under 5 years at 17.5%. Adenovirus positivity increased slightly to 1.6%, with the highest positivity in those aged under 5 years at 8.4%. Human metapneumovirus ( hMPV ) positivity increased to 0.7%, with the highest positivity in those aged under 5 years at 2.0%. Parainfluenza positivity increased to 3.6%, with the highest positivity in those aged between 5 and 14 years at 13.5%. Rhinovirus positivity decreased slightly to 14.6%, with the highest positivity in those aged under 5 years at 31.6%. DataMart data is provisional and subject to retrospective updates. Note 5: shading represents 95% confidence intervals. UKHSA conducts genomic surveillance of SARS-CoV-2 lineages. This section provides an overview of circulating lineages in England, derived from data on sequenced PCR -positive SARS-CoV-2 samples in SGSS . The prevalence of UKHSA -designated lineages among sequenced cases is presented in Figure 13. To account for reporting delays, we report the proportion of lineages within COVID-19 cases that have had a sequenced positive sample between 28 September 2026 and 11 October 2026. Note that low sequencing numbers, especially within the latest reporting period, will impact the accuracy of the prevalence estimates. These most recent figures should therefore be interpreted with caution. Note that lineages will be grouped independently from their parent lineage once they reach sufficient prevalence, and may be re-grouped into their parent lineage if their prevalence subsequently falls. The data quality report contains more information on lineage groupings. Analysis of viruses from primary and secondary care shows that circulating A(H1N1)pdm09 viruses show low genetic diversity and all belong to clade D.3.1.1. analysis.time: The report is based on data up to week 44 of 2026 (26 October to 1 November 2026) [N5].
analysis.location_and_population: The report covers England, focusing on influenza, RSV, and SARS-CoV-2 (COVID-19) activity across various populations, including those aged 65 years and over, individuals in clinical risk groups, and those aged 2 and 3 years [N4].
analysis.event: The report summarizes surveillance data for influenza, RSV, and SARS-CoV-2 in England, noting that influenza activity is above baseline levels, RSV activity is at baseline levels, and SARS-CoV-2 activity has decreased and is circulating at low levels [N4, N19, N24].
analysis.scale_impact_and_risk: Influenza ED attendances increased slightly and were above seasonally expected levels, while the number of influenza-confirmed ARI incidents decreased compared with the previous week. For SARS-CoV-2, ED attendances for COVID-19-like illness remained stable, and confirmed ARI incidents decreased. RSV ED attendances increased and were within seasonally expected levels [N7, N8, N20, N21, N25].
analysis.response_status_and_uncertainty: The report indicates that influenza activity is now above baseline levels, and a briefing note has been issued to inform the NHS. analysis.brief_en: The National Flu and COVID-19 Surveillance Report for 5 November 2026 (week 45) provides an overview of respiratory virus activity in England. It notes that influenza is circulating at low levels, with ED attendances for influenza-like illness slightly above seasonally expected levels. SARS-CoV-2 (COVID-19) activity has decreased, with confirmed acute respiratory infection (ARI) incidents declining compared to the previous week. RSV activity increased and is at baseline levels. The report highlights data collection challenges, including misclassification of pharmacy vaccinations and incomplete data in weeks 41 and 42, which have been corrected since week 43. A briefing note was issued to inform the NHS about influenza activity exceeding baseline levels. The data is based on the Moving Epidemic Method (MEM) and Mean Standard Deviation (MSD) for defining activity thresholds, with the latter now used for influenza and SARS-CoV-2 laboratory surveillance. The unified sample dataset (USD) is used to calculate SARS-CoV-2 test positivity rates, which decreased slightly in week 44 to 7.6% compared to 8.1% the previous week. Positivity rates remained stable among those aged 85 years and over, at 11.1%.

RSV ED attendances increased and were within seasonally expected levels [N7, N8, N20, N21, N25].
analysis_en.response_status_and_uncertainty: The report indicates that influenza activity is now above baseline levels, and a briefing note has been issued to inform the NHS. There are noted issues with data collection, including misclassification of pharmacy vaccinations and incomplete data in weeks 41 and 42, which have been corrected since week 43 [N9, N10, N11, N13, N14, N15].

news.title_zh: National flu and COVID-19 surveillance report: 5 November 2026 (week 45) - GOV.UK
news.source_body_en: The National Flu and COVID-19 Surveillance Report for 5 November 2026 (week 45) provides an overview of respiratory virus activity in England. It notes that influenza is circulating at low levels, with ED attendances for influenza-like illness slightly above seasonally expected levels. SARS-CoV-2 (COVID-19) activity has decreased, with confirmed acute respiratory infection (ARI) incidents declining compared to the previous week. RSV activity increased and is at baseline levels. The report highlights data collection challenges, including misclassification of pharmacy vaccinations and incomplete data in weeks 41 and 42, which have been corrected since week 43. A briefing note was issued to inform the NHS about influenza activity exceeding baseline levels. The data is based on the Moving Epidemic Method (MEM) and Mean Standard Deviation (MSD) for defining activity thresholds, with the latter now used for influenza and SARS-CoV-2 laboratory surveillance. The unified sample dataset (USD) is used to calculate SARS-CoV-2 test positivity rates, which decreased slightly in week 44 to 7.6% compared to 8.1% the previous week. Positivity rates remained stable among those aged 85 years and over, at 11.1%.

Careers Internships & Fellowships Apprenticeships & Workforce Development Work at DOE Funding Opportunities Breadcrumb Biological and Environmental Research Redesigned Hepatitis C Drug Becomes a Powerful New Treatment for COVID-19 Redesigned Hepatitis C Drug Becomes a Powerful New Treatment for COVID-19 Scientists transformed an old drug into a potent COVID-19 treatment effective against drug-resistant variants. Biological and Environmental Research February 19, 2026 Estimated Read Time 3 min The final version of the redesigned drug binds tightly to the main COVID-19 protease, an enzyme the virus needs to multiply. The drug’s structure is effective even against mutated forms that resist other treatments. Image courtesy of Stanford University The Science Researchers have redesigned the hepatitis C drug boceprevir to create a more effective treatment for COVID-19. Some virus variants no longer respond well to current therapies, like Paxlovid, due to mutations in the main COVID-19 virus protease (Mpro). This is a key enzyme the virus uses to replicate. Mpro is essential to the virus and remains intact from variant to variant. As such, it is an ideal target for treatments to focus on. Using X-ray crystal structures, scientists refined boceprevir atom by atom. They worked to improve how the drug binds within key pockets of the enzyme. The researchers used the Stanford Synchrotron Radiation Lightsource (a DOE Office of Science User Facility) to analyze the crystal structure when the drug was attached to Mpro. The Impact This research produced a drug that is effective against COVID-19 strains that are resistant to existing treatments. The resulting compound, ML2006a4, binds more tightly and durably than earlier drugs. It also shows superior protection in preclinical animal studies. By redesigning an older hepatitis C drug, scientists made it more effective against mutated forms of the virus’s protease. This could help doctors treat patients who no longer respond to existing therapies. Summary Boceprevir is a protease inhibitor originally developed to treat hepatitis C. Scientists adapted this drug to target the main protease (Mpro) of SARS-CoV-2. This is a critical enzyme the virus uses to process its polyproteins and replicate. Because Mpro is conserved across variants and has no close human equivalent, it remains a prime target for antiviral drug development. However, some SARS-CoV-2 variants contain mutations in Mpro that reduce the effectiveness of existing treatments. Using X-ray crystallography data collected at the Macromolecular Crystallography Beamlines at the Stanford Synchrotron Radiation Lightsource (SSRL), researchers determined high-resolution structures of Mpro bound to various boceprevir analogs. These structural insights guided a stepwise redesign of the molecule to improve its fit within the enzyme’s active site and sub-pockets. The team optimized interactions and reduced internal strains within the drug’s structure to improve binding, potency, and resistance profile. The final compound, ML2006a4, binds covalently to Mpro and retains strong activity even against variants harboring resistance-associated mutations. This structure-guided approach demonstrates how iterative design can yield next-generation antivirals with broad-spectrum activity. It also underscores the vital role of DOE- and NIH-supported synchrotron-based methods in accelerating drug discovery against emerging viral threats. Contact Michael Lin Stanford University mzlin@stanford.edu Funding Funding for this research included: Sarafan ChEM-H and the Innovative Medicines Accelerator, Harrington Scholar-Innovator Award, Emergent Ventures at the Mercatus Center at George Mason University, Stanford-Coulter Translational Research Grant, National Institute of Health(NIH)/National Institute of Allergy and Infectious Diseases (NIAID) Antiviral Drug Discovery (AViDD) Center, the Denver Foundation, the Novo Nordisk Foundation, the Stanford Bio-X Program and a Bio-X Interdisciplinary Graduate Student Fellowship, E&M Foundation Postdoctoral Fellowship, Postdoctoral Fellowship in Translational Medicine from the PhRMA Foundation and an anonymous donation to establish the Stanford BSL3 facility. The research used resources at SSRL, a DOE Office of Science user facility, and of the SSRL Structural Molecular Biology Program supported by the DOE Office of Biological and Environmental Research and by NIH National Institute of General Medical Sciences. Publications Westberg, M., et al. “An orally bioavailable SARS-CoV-2 main protease inhibitor exhibits improved affinity and reduced sensitivity to mutations”, Sci. Transl. Med. 16, eadi0979 (2024). Circulation Cases Deaths Hospitalizations Vaccines Variants Wastewater Data About More resources More COVID-19 Cases, %%COUNTRY%% WHO will utilize various sources to continue monitoring the COVID-19 epidemiological situation via the WHO COVID-19 dashboard. If data for certain countries is unavailable in this section, it may indicate that they have either ceased reporting COVID-19 surveillance data to WHO or have integrated the COVID-19 surveillance into existing respiratory disease surveillance. In the latter case, SARS-CoV-2 detections from sentinel and systematic virological surveillance sites in those countries may be found in the Circulation section which also includes information on SARS-CoV-2 variant circulation. This global summary of COVID-19 cases includes data on confirmed cases reported to WHO from the comprehensive COVID-19 case monitoring. Coronavirus (COVID-19) cases, %%COUNTRY%% data Source: World Health Organization Loading... Loading... Loading... What is the definition of 'confirmed' and 'reported' in COVID-19 data? All data represents the date of reporting as opposed to date of symptom onset. All data is subject to continuous verification and may change based on retrospective updates to accurately reflect trends, changes in country case definitions and/or reporting practices. Significant data errors detected or reported to WHO may be corrected at more frequent intervals with some countries performing retrospective bulk corrections may lead to the appearance of significant spikes or negative values which are verified and validated by WHO. In the context of WHO's statistical reporting of COVID-19 data, it is important to note that only confirmed cases are included in case and death counts. In guidance updated on 22 July 2023; there are two alternative definitions for 'Confirmed case of SARS-CoV-2 infection' in international surveillance reporting, although some departures may exist due to local adaptations: a) A person with a positive Nucleic Acid Amplification Test (NAAT), regardless of clinical criteria OR epidemiological criteria. b) A person meeting clinical criteria AND/OR epidemiological criteria (suspect case A) with a positive professional-use or self-test SARS-CoV-2 Antigen-RDT. Additionally, WHO only disseminates data as reported by its Member States. From the 31 December 2019 to the 21 March 2020, WHO collected the numbers of confirmed COVID-19 cases and deaths through official communications under the International Health Regulations (IHR, 2005), complemented by monitoring the official ministries of health websites and social media accounts. Since 22 March 2020, global data has been compiled through WHO region-specific dashboards, and/or aggregate count data reported directly to WHO headquarters by Member States. Statistical counts include both domestic and repatriated cases. Case detection, definitions, testing strategies, reporting practice, and lag times (e.g. time to case notification, and time to reporting of deaths) differ between countries, territories and areas. These factors, amongst others, influence the counts presented with variable under or overestimation of true case and death counts, and variable delays to reflecting these statistics at a global level. Please note that statistics do not necessarily reflect the actual number of cases and deaths or the actual number of countries where cases and deaths are occurring, as a number of countries have stopped reporting or changed their frequency of reporting. Trends in COVID-19 cases, %%COUNTRY%% Recent COVID-19 cases reported to WHO (weekly) %%COUNTRY%%, July 2023 - present Source: World Health Organization Data may be incomplete for the latest week. Total COVID-19 cases reported to WHO (weekly) %%COUNTRY%%, January 2020 - present Source: World Health Organization Why is COVID-19 data being presented as weekly statistics? A number of countries have stopped reporting or changed their frequency of reporting COVID-19 case and death counts to WHO. An outcome of these differences in reporting is that WHO may receive daily data from some countries, while other countries may only report data to WHO once every 14 days. In addition, countries differ in how they choose to report statistics; some countries provide their data attributed to specific dates while others who report less frequently may group data from 7 days into a single statistic attributed to a week in their reporting. As of 25 August 2023, WHO declared that it is no longer necessary for Member States to report daily counts of cases and deaths to WHO and requested strengthening of weekly reporting. Reported data is still available attributed to specific dates (daily data) here as a download. This dashboard presents the same statistics as weekly figures in charts in order to mitigate against the visual misinterpretation of data. Should daily data have been presented here, many countries would show zero counts for multiple consecutive days due in part to the differences in how they choose to report. While weekly intervals do not completely mitigate against this, the approach reduces the risk that some dashboard users might infer zero cases or deaths when lack of data is often due to reporting differences. What do negative counts of cases or deaths mean? All data is subject to continuous verification and may change based on retrospective updates to accurately reflect trends, changes in country case definitions and/or reporting practices. Significant data errors detected or reported to WHO may be corrected by Member States at more frequent intervals with some countries performing retrospective bulk corrections in their reporting. Bulk corrections may lead to the appearance of significant spikes or negative values which are verified and validated by WHO. Apply Departments Biochemistry and Molecular Biology Biostatistics Environmental Health and Engineering Epidemiology Health Policy and Management Health, Behavior and Society International Health Mental Health Molecular Microbiology and Immunology Population, Family and Reproductive Health Faculty Topics Bloomberg School What to Know About Flu, COVID-19, and RSV This Fall Influenza activity is increasing, while RSV and COVID case numbers remain low. Published November 04, 2026 By Morgan Coulson COVID-19 Infectious Diseases Medicine Vaccines As we head into the late fall and winter months, flu cases are beginning to rise in parts of the U.S., even as overall respiratory virus activity remains low. The CDC is predicting a relatively moderate respiratory virus season, similar to last year’s, when weekly hospitalizations from flu, COVID-19, and RSV peaked at around 16 per 100,000 people. But that’s no reason to put off vaccination, explains Andrew Pekosz, PhD, a professor in Molecular Microbiology and Immunology: “This is a good last call to get your influenza vaccination for this year, because vaccines work best when taken before the influenza season starts.” This season also brings a new option for some adults: a recently approved mRNA influenza vaccine for people ages 50 and older. “The hope is that the new mRNA vaccine will produce a better immune response against influenza and, therefore, provide better protection,” says Anna Durbin, MD, a professor in International Health and director of the Center for Immunization Research. In this Q&A, adapted from an October 29 media briefing, Pekosz and Durbin discuss emerging respiratory virus trends, what we know about this season’s vaccines, and how people can protect themselves and others as the season progresses. What is the current situation with influenza in the United States? Andrew Pekosz: Influenza activity is low but increasing, particularly in the western and southern U.S. This is early, but not unheard of. The cases seem to be driven by a variant of the H1N1 influenza virus, which has some new mutations compared with last year’s H1N1 virus. Those mutations allow it to escape some of the immunity in the population. However, data suggest this year’s influenza vaccine can recognize this variant. Influenza vaccines cover three different viruses, and usually different influenza viruses cause infections at the beginning and end of the flu season. So, even if you hear about a potential mismatch with the H1N1 component, it’s important to get the vaccine because the other two components look like they’re going to be pretty good matches for the viruses emerging early in the flu season. How well do this season’s COVID and RSV vaccines match the strains circulating now? AP: For COVID, we’re seeing low but steady activity. We expect another increase in cases sometime in December or January. We haven’t seen much RSV activity this year, which is somewhat unusual. However, I expect we’ll begin seeing RSV cases in the next couple of weeks. Now is the time to get your COVID and RSV vaccines, if you’re eligible, along with influenza and pneumococcal vaccines, to prepare for the respiratory virus season. Both the COVID and RSV vaccines are very good matches for the viruses currently circulating. The RSV vaccine is recommended for a more limited group of individuals, particularly those ages 75 and older, as well as people with certain underlying conditions or who are immunocompromised. That vaccine has demonstrated very good efficacy over the past few years. [Note: The RSV vaccine is not currently an annual vaccine, per the CDC.] What’s the difference between the new mRNA flu vaccine and the traditional vaccine? Anna Durbin: Essentially, the mRNA vaccine enters your cells and instructs them to make the flu protein against which your body produces antibodies. The cells make that protein and then present it to your immune system, exposing the immune system to the protein, or antigen. Current traditional flu vaccines, by contrast, contain proteins that stimulate an immune response. Unlike mRNA vaccines, they don’t enter the cells in the same way to stimulate the broadest possible immune response. Traditional vaccines generate a good antibody response but may not stimulate other parts of the immune system as effectively as mRNA vaccines do. Which is more effective? AD: We don’t have data from the current flu season yet. However, the clinical trials used to support the mRNA vaccine’s approval showed that, in people ages 50 and older, it performed better than traditional vaccines. One important consideration is that adults ages 65 and older receive a higher dose of the traditional flu vaccines than younger people. The mRNA vaccine was not directly compared in clinical trials with those high-dose vaccines in people ages 65 and older. However, we know that the antibody responses generated by the mRNA flu vaccine in people ages 65 and older were at least as good as those generated by traditional flu vaccines. Until we get good real-world efficacy data from the flu season, we won’t know for sure. How is the mRNA vaccine different from a public health standpoint? AD: The advantage of an mRNA influenza vaccine is that it can be produced very quickly. For instance, if a new strain emerges over the summer, the [fall] vaccine [for that year] could potentially be changed to match it. Right now, the FDA holds a meeting every March to select which strains will be included in the influenza vaccine. That meeting happens so early because it takes a long time to produce traditional influenza vaccines. The hope with an mRNA vaccine is that we might be able to hold another meeting in July or August and update the vaccine if the circulating strains have changed. We’re not there yet. The agency is discussing and exploring that possibility, and I think a lot will depend on the evidence generated by this new mRNA influenza vaccine. How can a person tell whether they have the flu, COVID, a cold, or something else? AP: Usually, you can distinguish a cold from something more significant or serious by the effect it has on your ability to breathe and by the severity of your cough. If you have difficulty breathing, that can mean the infection is spreading deeper into your lungs. In that case, it may not be a common cold but one of the other respiratory viruses. There are some useful at-home testing kits that can help determine whether you're infected with influenza, RSV, or COVID-19. Knowing which virus you have is particularly important if you’re in a high-risk group for severe illness. Antiviral treatments are available for influenza and COVID-19, and they have been shown to reduce the duration of symptoms and the likelihood of developing severe illness. The key is that you need to start these antivirals soon after symptoms begin. Be proactive. Keep some at-home tests available, and if you test positive for one of these viruses, contact your pharmacy to make sure you can get the appropriate antiviral medication and begin taking it as soon as possible. What should immunocompromised people and adults ages 65 and older do this fall? AD: Immunocompromised people and adults older than 65 should get vaccinated. We also know from many studies that adults over 65 often get infected by their grandchildren and other children. Get young children vaccinated against influenza, not only for older adults’ protection but also because influenza can cause serious complications in children, including death. How long after vaccination does it take for protection to develop? AP: It takes about two weeks for influenza vaccine protection to reach its maximum level. That protection then lasts for several weeks to several months after vaccination. Getting vaccinated before influenza becomes widespread will provide the greatest protection against disease. What is the most important thing for primary care physicians to know about this flu season? AD: Influenza can be a very serious illness. The CDC reported almost 5,000 laboratory-confirmed influenza hospitalizations nationwide during the week ending October 17. This is the highest early-season hospitalization rate for mid-October since the 2010–2011 flu season. [The following week, ending October 24, that number rose to 6,100 hospitalizations nationwide, according to the CDC.] I think it’s really important, particularly for older adults who are at greater risk of severe influenza, to get vaccinated. What I tell my patients, and what I encourage other physicians to tell their patients, is that a flu vaccine is the best way to protect yourself against influenza, and to get vaccinated as soon as possible. Fewer people are getting the flu vaccine, or they are getting it later in the season. What is the impact of this? AD: We do think that, overall, fewer people are getting vaccinated against various diseases, which increases the risk of infection. Unfortunately, when fewer people get vaccinated, influenza can spread more easily, resulting in more infections and potentially serious consequences for people’s health. There are a lot of questions people have about vaccines, and there’s been a lot of misinformation circulating. I encourage people to talk with their physicians. supplementary_news.excerpt: Genomic sequencing of 535 SARS-CoV-2 samples from Duhok, Iraq, shows the Delta variant arrived three months before a targeted travel ban and Omicron entered despite restrictions already in force.
